causalModel.founding: The assembly designated this Hist for tapping and issued a licence against it, for a single stage on the tree for one season. The stage stands where the crew could raise it without cutting into the root flare.
causalModel.siteAdvantages: A firm terrace at 30.7 to 31.4 m under a closed canopy, rising to the hut pad at 32.7 m, with the road 526 m to the south-west. The water is not here. The reach below the camp falls 29 m in 460 m and stands in pockets. The canoe lies 370 m away at the head of the tide, where the surface runs dead level and the dredged creek carries 0.84 m for 358 m to the coast.
causalModel.occupantsMotive: A tapper and two crew whose licence is their livelihood. They keep the stage correct and police poachers themselves, because a district that cannot police itself loses its licences.
causalModel.pressures: The licence is renewed annually and the objection comes most reliably from the tribe whose tree carried the stage last year. The lay-by is out of sight of the camp and out of earshot. Night landings there are not the crew's work.
causalModel.wouldChangeIf: A licence revoked would empty the stage within a season and leave the lay-by to whoever poles up to it.

districts.notes: The tapping stage on the Hist's channel face, its stair, the mule line, the season's stock and the licence board at the head of the sap track. Works set only (stockade scaffold at one side count, the BM&V notice board).

why.what: The works: the stage and its stair against the Hist's channel face, the mule line, the season's cart and the licence board where the track to the water leaves the camp.
why.whyHere: Sap is drawn where the tree stands; the stage is raised against the trunk and everything that serves it stays within a few paces.
why.whyNeighbours: It lies between the hut to the east and the fall to the west, so the crew walk through the works both to their beds and to the track down to their boat; the board stands at its western end, where that track starts.
why.playerPurpose: The climbable stage, the tapper, the graded stock and the licence, all within thirty paces of each other.
why.microGeography: The terrace here runs 30.7 to 31.4 m, with a 1.26 m fall under the stage that the scaffold posts take and a longer fall to the south-west that the sap track uses.

districts.notes: One mud-hut dwelling behind the trunk, the crew's hearth clutter and the spur off the track. Mud-culture set only; never blended with the works props on the stage.

why.what: The camp: one hut, its hearth clutter and the spur off the track.
why.whyHere: A season's crew sleep beside their stage. The stage stands at the tree.
why.whyNeighbours: The hut stands behind the trunk from the works, so a visitor meets the stage first and the sleeping place last.
why.playerPurpose: The hut is the camp's only interior. The crew sleep in it through the night landing that MR04 stages at the lay-by.
why.microGeography: The hut pad sits at 32.7 m, the highest ground in the camp. From it the ground falls west and south toward the creek.

routes.why: The single worn line into the camp, worn from the south-east. The heartland network reaches the stage across the flat, so the track meets the camp at its lower head. It bends round the hut and mule line, then hooks north-west to die squarely at the scaffold stair's open foot.

The carry path down to the water. The camp stands 30.8 m above the tide and the nearest water that a canoe can travel is 370 m to the south-south-west, so the sap is carried down on a crewman's back. It is a footpath rather than a track because one pitch falls a quarter, which no mule descends under load; the mules take the road instead. The line starts at the stage foot, passes the licence board six paces below it and ends on the bank at the head of the plank walk.
The worn spur from the track to the hut's door: three strides that the crew take every night.

canals.why: The last 23 m of the poling line, coming up the creek from the south between mud and reed and ending at the piles. Above the piles the reach falls too steeply for poling.

boardwalks.why: The plank walk from the bank down to the landing, 11.7 m laid over mud and reed so a tin is carried dry off the sap track and into the canoe.

parcels.orientationWhy: Turned so the scaffold's one unrailed face looks along bearing 136 to the Hist trunk, where the tap lines run. The three railed faces stand outward.

why.what: The tapping stage: a three-sided stockade scaffold footing with its deck at 2.7 m, whose open face looks at the trunk.
why.whyHere: A tapping stage is the structure that the licence requires; the tap lines run from the tree to its deck.
why.whySpot: It stands 9.8 m off the trunk centre on the channel face, clear of the root flare, where the crew could raise it without cutting into a root.
why.whyNeighbours: The stair joins it on the landward side, the root flare lies between it and the trunk. The sap track leaves from a stride off its foot.
why.playerPurpose: The stage that MR04 asks the player to climb and search; the tapper stands above it by day.
why.microGeography: The ground under the footing falls 1.26 m toward the water, which is why it stands on its own posts rather than on a cut pad.

parcels.orientationWhy: The flight is set with its west face on the stage's south face, so the stair is built into the stage. The climb still starts on the landward side at the head of the track, clear of the water.

why.what: The scaffold stair, 3.45 m of rise, that climbs to the deck from the landward side.
why.whyHere: A deck at 2.7 m needs a way up. The crew carry full vessels down it.
why.whySpot: At the head of the track. The climb starts where the walk from the road ends, on dry ground.
why.whyNeighbours: The track ends against its lowest tread; the mule line stands beside the track a few paces back.
why.playerPurpose: The visible means of ascent: from the last bend of the track the stair is in frame, so the player knows how to reach the deck.
why.microGeography: The ground under the flight falls 0.89 m, so it stands on posts like the footing.

parcels.abutsWhy: The stockade scaffold stair is the kit's own way up to the scaffold footing: its top tread lands on the deck edge, so the two pieces were made to touch.

parcels.orientationWhy: The trough's long axis lies north to south, along the track's last stretch, so the mules stand beside the path rather than across it.

why.what: A trough and the tie line for the two mules that carry the season's sap to the road.
why.whyHere: Sap goes out by mule when the channel is watched, so the crew keep the animals at the camp.
why.whySpot: Beside the last straight of the track, a dozen paces short of the stair, where a loaded mule can be tied without standing in the path.
why.whyNeighbours: Nine paces from the cart, on the track side, so a load is carried from cart to mule along the path. Nothing stands between the stair and the stage.
why.playerPurpose: Mules at a camp that also keeps a landing show that sap leaves by two routes.
why.microGeography: On a gentle pad at 31.3 m, where the track straightens for its run to the stair.

parcels.orientationWhy: The cart's shafts point on bearing 35 toward the track, so the season's stock is pulled out without turning it.

why.what: The handcart that holds the season's packed and graded stock.
why.whyHere: The recipe's gated reward: sap sold by weight has to be graded and packed somewhere before it moves.
why.whySpot: Ten paces off the stage foot, clear of the stair, with the shafts to the track, so a full cart is pulled out without turning.
why.whyNeighbours: It stands between the stage foot and the mule line, nine paces from each, so a load goes to the plank walk or to the mules along a clear path.
why.playerPurpose: The container socket of MR04 and the camp's one item of value.
why.microGeography: On a plinth at the edge of the level pad, 31.2 m, two metres above the channel's wet-season line.

playerPurpose.note: The graded tins at issue in Sap for Sale. They are the goods of value that the camp holds.

parcels.orientationWhy: The hut has one doorway. Turned to 113.0°, it looks out at 225° onto the tent spur, the path the tapper walks twice a day.

playerPurpose.note: The crew sleep through the night landing that MR04 stages; one of them wakes.
The crew's own graded stock, kept off the stage where the licence does not count it.
The season's tally is written up here. It records less sap than has left by canoe.

why.what: A small Argonian mud hut with one doorway, where the crew of three sleep.
why.whyHere: The same crew work the licence season after season, so they keep a mud hut rather than a tent.
why.whySpot: The flattest pad in the camp, behind the trunk from the stage, so a visitor reaches the works before the sleeping place.
why.whyNeighbours: Its one doorway looks down the track, so the crew see who comes up it; its blind back stands to the channel.
why.playerPurpose: The camp's only interior. Inside are the crew's beds, their own stock and the season's tally.
why.microGeography: On a plinth over a 0.71 m fall, at 32.7 m, the highest ground in the camp.

parcels.orientationWhy: The pane stands across the sap track on bearing 109, so its face looks on bearing 199 down the line to the water. Whoever climbs the 370 m from the landing reads the licence before the stage comes into frame.

why.what: The licence board: a roofed notice pane on two posts, with the licence and its counter-signature pinned under the roof.
why.whyHere: The licence runs against the tree, so it hangs at the tree. The water is 370 m off and the stage cannot be seen from it, so a board on the bank down there would license nothing an inspector could see.
why.whySpot: On the terrace at 30.8 m, where the track down to the landing leaves the camp. Every load of sap passes it leaving the camp; every visitor passes it arriving.
why.whyNeighbours: It stands ten paces west of the stock cart and eight west of the mule line, clear of both, with the stage and its stair behind it to the east.
why.playerPurpose: The evidence socket of MR04: the counter-signature that the player matches elsewhere.
why.microGeography: Two posts driven into the terrace lip at 30.8 m, at the point where the ground begins its fall to the creek.

playerPurpose.note: The counter-signature on the board is the evidence Sap for Sale matches elsewhere.

parcels.orientationWhy: Turned with its footing, so its three rails sit over the footing's three railed sides and the open side matches.

why.what: The stage deck: the railed three-sided top tier of the tapping stage, stacked on its footing.
why.whyHere: The works kit's own grammar: a three-sided top on a three-sided base, the tier that makes the footing a deck with rails.
why.whySpot: On the footing against the Hist's channel face, so the tapper works at the rails with the trunk on the open side.
why.whyNeighbours: It stands on its footing. The stair on the footing's landward face reaches it.
why.playerPurpose: The railed deck to which the player climbs. Graded sap is sold from it; the stage keeps no other counter.
why.microGeography: Carried on the footing's posts at 2.7 m; it touches no ground.

parcels.abutsWhy: The stockade stair is authored to land on the stockade deck; the deck's rail line meets the stair's top tread.

playerPurpose.note: The anchor roster of Sap for Sale is read off the selling deck.

landmarks.assetRef: htbm:here there be monsters - curse of cipactli/trees/histtree
landmarks.notes: The licensed tree. Measured bounds 64.0 x 45.3 m across the crown, 53.6 m tall, 17073 tris. The stage stands 9.8 m off the trunk centre on the channel face; trunk clearance is verified against the geometry at Round B before the stage is fixed. Yaw 121 lays the crown's long axis (64.0 m) on bearing 211, across the channel, so the deepest shade falls over the stage and the landing rather than along the water.

why.what: The licensed Hist: the largest Hist mesh in the vault, 64 m across the crown and 53.6 m tall.
why.whyHere: The tree is the reason for the place; the assembly designated it and the licence runs against it.
why.whySpot: It stands on the north-east bank of the channel at the head of the terrace, where its root plate is above the flood and its channel face looks down on the poling water.
why.whyNeighbours: The stage is raised on its channel face and the hut stands behind it. The crown shades both the works and the landing.
why.playerPurpose: The beacon: the crown shows above the canopy from the road and from the channel. It is the mark toward which the player walks and paddles.
why.microGeography: Rooted at 32.1 m on the terrace lip, with the crown's long axis laid across the channel on bearing 211.

landmarks.assetRef: htbm:here there be monsters - curse of cipactli/trees/histroots03
landmarks.notes: Root flare from the same author's set, laid between the trunk and the stage footing; 9.56 x 2.54 m, 4.71 m high. Yaw 46 lays its 9.56 m axis on the trunk-to-stage line (bearing 136), which is the line that a flare out of the root plate would follow.

why.what: A root flare from the same author's set, laid between the trunk and the stage footing.
why.whyHere: A great tree's roots break the ground for metres around it. The stage was raised where a flare could be stepped over rather than cut.
why.whySpot: On the trunk-to-stage line, bearing 136, the line that a flare out of the root plate would follow.
why.whyNeighbours: It separates the footing from the trunk, which is why the stage stands 9.8 m off the centre and not closer.
why.playerPurpose: Cover at the stage foot: a player crouched behind the flare is out of the tapper's line from the deck.
why.microGeography: 4.7 m high and 9.6 m long, it lies along the fall so the ground on either side of it drains to the water.

docks.assetRef: htbm:here there be monsters - curse of cipactli/architecture/villages/kothringi/tamu_wooddock01
docks.notes: The landing faces bearing 65, back up the plank walk, so a canoe poling up the creek from the south lies alongside the piles and unloads onto the bank.

why.what: The landing: a piled stage at the head of the tide, where the crew's canoe lies.
why.whyHere: Sap leaves by water. The water that a canoe can use is not at the camp. Above this point the reach falls 29 m in 460 m and stands in pockets a hull cannot pass. Here the surface is dead level at 0.05 m and the sea is 1.40 km off. The tide reaches no further inland than these piles.
why.whySpot: The piles stand in 0.84 m of compiled water on a bed 0.80 m below the surface, at the last cell of the creek that carries a canoe. Five metres north the surface climbs to 0.96 m and the creek becomes a fall. The berth is the head of navigation; it cannot be moved further up.
why.whyNeighbours: Nothing else stands here. The plank walk runs 11.7 m to the dry bank at 1.35 m. The sap track climbs from that bank to the camp. The lay-by is left unmarked.
why.playerPurpose: The arrival point for a player who comes by canoe. It is the far end of the walk down from the stage. The night landing in MR04 is staged here.
why.microGeography: Piled to the bed at the head of the tide, in a dead-level creek that runs 358 m to the coast, with a low mud bank on its east side and reeds on its west.

docks.fixedBerthReason: The water fixes the berth. This is the highest cell of the creek that floats a canoe, and the ground above it is a falling reach.

combatSpaces.why: MR04's night landing is watched from the reeds at the lay-by; a carrier who is followed up the track brings the woken crew down the stair to this ground. The licence-revoked flip makes the same crew hostile by day. The stage foot is the widest ground in the camp. The space is tight.

doors.notes: The door sits on the hut's measured doorway; the blank wall stands opposite, to the channel. The interior is the hut's own volume, dressed from settlement-mud-v1 rather than held as a separate cell.

assetConstraints: stockade-scaffold pieces at one side count (base3sided + stairs + top3sided), per works-v1 snapLogic; the top tier is placed as a stacked parcel on the footing
no settlement-root dwelling pieces here: the smallest root house measures 24.6 x 24.6 m and 55.6 m tall
the stage carries no metal fixings; hardwood pegs and withy only
the licence board is bmv:advertising_board from works-v1, pane to the water; no other notice piece exists in the vault

candidates.why: The bank above the head of reach 118. Anchor ground 31.20 m, flood band 0, buildable 59% of the 150 m disc; every parcel stands dry: stage 30.67 m, stair 31.38 m, cart 31.20 m, mule line 31.27 m, hut 32.65 m, licence board 30.81 m. Road 526 m to the south-west. Canopy closure 1.00; concealment 0.74. The camp keeps this bank. Its landing stands elsewhere. The water at the foot of the camp is an 882 m2 pocket bounded x 3327-3433, z 4453-4507, connected to nothing, on a reach that falls 6.3% over 463 m, so a canoe floating there can go nowhere. The berth moved 357 m on bearing 201 to (3309.4, 4815.0), the head of the tide, which the recipe's satellite slot already asks for at 200 to 400 m. See dossier licensed-stage-layby.
The siting this place held until 2026-09-09, chosen on the macro hydrology raster, which reported a 0.9 m channel 16 m to the NNW.
candidates.rejectedBecause: Measured against the compiled water that ships, the berth stands on dry terrace at 30.52 m and the nearest water carrying a canoe's 0.6 m is 104.4 m away. The ground between rises up to 1.48 m above the local water for 92 continuous metres, so no dredge can reach it. The berth published no connector and the network gate stayed red.

candidates.why: The flattest ground on this bank: slope 4.94 deg at the dot, 5.88 m of relief across a 30 m disc, all of it dry.
candidates.rejectedBecause: The berth it implies sits on an 11.0 deg bank 0.25 m above the surface, with the poling water 8.0 m off, which is beyond the reach of the 3.6 by 1.83 m dock piece, so the deck would end over mud. The camp would also stand 7.8 m above its water table, putting the licence board a climb above anyone arriving by canoe.

candidates.why: Two metres from the chosen point and slightly nearer the water: the berth would lie 4.53 m from 0.6 m water at 0.39 m above the surface.
candidates.rejectedBecause: Two metres of gain buys nothing. The water below it is the same dead pocket. The bank measures 7.5 deg, too steep for piles to stand level.

needs: the licence itself, legible in the world and carrying a counter-signature the player can match elsewhere
a stage a player can climb and search without combat
a channel bank where a night landing can be watched from cover

scaleGrounding.loreSource: type recipe sap-tapping-camp (population 2–5, an elevated member on the stage, a mule line); Lore:Hist Sap; world/sources/lore/topics/hist-placement.md §75 (a licence runs against the tree, for one season)
scaleGrounding.why: A licence is one stage on one tree for one season. One stage needs a tapper on the deck and two hands on the ground. Three people share a hut, keep a mule line and fill a cart. Three things are BUILT here — the stage, its stair and the hut — and the mule line, the cart and the licence board are the dressing that says what the three are for (97 C5b).

approaches.sequence: The Hist's crown shows above the jungle canopy from the low ground to the south-east, 400 m out along the worn line. The track then goes under closed canopy and the crown is lost. The pale trunk reads between the other trunks at about 30 m. The hut's door and the mule line appear at the first bend. The stair and the stage come into frame at the second.
approaches.wayfinding: Follow the one worn line north-west off the road toward the great tree. Keep on until it bends twice at the camp and ends at the foot of the stair.
approaches.notes: The track is 416 m long and joins the heartland network at (3654.8, 4751.5), 349 m to the south-east; the Helstrom-Blackrose road runs 526 m to the south-west as the crow flies. The last 27 m bend twice, round the hut and past the mule line, so the stage is seen, lost behind the trunk and found again. Canopy closure over the camp is 1.00 and the dossier measures concealment at 0.74. The camp is in view from 26% of the route points within two kilometres, against a fourteenth of them at the terrace the place left. A walker on the track steers by the crown rather than by anything built. The carry path leaves the same ground on the other side. It passes the licence board and drops to the water.

approaches.sequence: The Hist's crown stands over the jungle to the north-east from a bend away; the reeds hide the east bank until 20 m; the piles and the plank walk open up at the head of the creek; the bank above them is empty; the track that climbs from it is not seen until a boat is alongside.
approaches.wayfinding: Pole up the creek toward the great tree and come alongside the piles where the water ends. Take the plank walk to the bank and follow the track up; it climbs 29.5 m in 370 and dies at the licence board, with the stage beyond it.
approaches.notes: The lay-by is unmarked. The licence hangs at the tree, 370 m up the track, so an inspector reads it after the climb rather than from the water. Concealment at the berth is 0.99: the road passes 209 m to the south-west and the landing is in view from 1% of the 817 route points within 2 km.

networkTerminals.why: The stage is licensed but not advertised. One worn line leaves the heartland network to the south-east and dies at the foot of the stair, which is where it reaches the camp. It is walked ground, so the path is routed and left off the map.

The camp's water link is the tidal creek at the foot of the reach, poled up from the network 380 m to the south. It ends at the piles at the head of the tide; the sap track carries the tins the remaining 370 m up to the camp.
